b: Writing documentation Every page of the documentation site is a Markdown file under docs/. The generator src/tools/docsite turns them into the static site under site/docs/. There is no framework and nothing is fetched at runtime; the pages render in Wren itself. The pages, their sidebar, search, Markdown, highlighter and link check are the toolkit's site package (ext/gui_toolkit/src/site, documented in ext/gui_toolkit/docs/site.md); src/tools/docsite gives it Wren's names, header, footer, colours, the WIDL language and the directives below, and makes the classic presentation. The site has a second, classic presentation under site/classic/ (plain links, one column of text, light and dark; site/classic/classic.css), reached by "Classic version" in every footer and back by "Modern version". The same tool makes it from the same sources: each doc is rendered a second time in the classic frame, and each hand-written page of the site (site/<page>/index.html) gives its <main> and its scripts, its links moved into the classic tree. Only the classic home, site/classic/index.html, is written by hand; its top, footer, version and release news are stamped between markers. So edit the modern page or the .md, never a generated classic page, and run wrentool docs. The workflow Write or edit a .md file under docs/. Accessibility Wren is read by screen readers (NVDA, Narrator, JAWS) and other assistive technologies through UI Automation. The toolkit makes the accessibility tree of the interface from its boxes and hands it to AccessKit (ext/gui_toolkit/docs/accessibility.md); Wren says what only a browser knows. Build The assembly crate native/wren_native builds the toolkit's adapter (ext/gui_toolkit/native/a11y, AccessKit 0.25 and its Windows adapter) into wren_native.lib (feature a11y: a program links one Rust static library; see docs/architecture.md, "The Rust library"), and build.bat builds with -define:A11Y_ACCESSKIT=true -define:A11Y_NATIVE_LINK=false. The crates are listed in native/rust-crates.txt (about:licenses). Nothing is built until an assistive technology asks for a window's tree; from then on each frame sends the nodes that changed. wren ctl stats --json says what was sent: a11yUpdates, a11yRefused, a11yLastNodes, a11yNodes. Web API of Wren (Wasm imports) Every function a page or worker module can import, generated from api/*.widl. The same description produces the host trampolines (src/page/api_generated.odin), the Odin guest SDK (sdk/odin), these pages and the conformance tests (examples/apiconformance, src/tools/apiconformance). The Odin SDK sdk/odin is a collection of packages, one per area of the API: a module, or the modules of one package below. Module async Promises, microtasks, buffers and host objects: the asynchronous core every other module builds on. A promise's value is an i64 (a number, or the handle of a buffer or another object) plus a string (an error message, a text result). Reactions run as microtasks once it settles. There are no closures in Wasm, so then does not create a chained promise: a reaction that passes a result on resolves a promise of its own. A buffer is the ArrayBuffer of this platform: bytes owned by the browser, passed between APIs without copies into the module's memory (fetch bodies, messages, socket frames), counted against page.max_fetch_bytes. Module canvas Canvas 2D (HTML §4.12.5): the 2D rendering context of canvas and OffscreenCanvas, drawn by a software rasterizer (package canvas2d) into a premultiplied RGBA8 bitmap that the shell shows as a texture, updated only when the drawing changed. Members shared by CanvasRenderingContext2D and OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D are one function imported under their mixin's name (CanvasState_save...); those of CanvasPath work on a context's current path or on a Path2D alike (CanvasPathTarget). Arguments that are NaN or infinite make a drawing or path call do nothing (the specification's rule); an enum given an invalid string leaves the attribute as it was. colors are CSS color strings, parsed by the browser's CSS parser (currentcolor is the canvas element's color); fillStyle / strokeStyle read back as #rrggbb or rgba(r, g, b, a); pixel data (ImageData) is straight-alpha RGBA8, rows top to bottom; a canvas that drew an image the page may not read (cross-origin without CORS) is tainted: reading it back (getImageData, toDataURL, toBlob...) raises Security; workers have OffscreenCanvas (drawn in the worker's thread; its text is not drawn yet: the shell's fonts belong to the interface thread); functions taking an element answer as for a dead handle there. Module credentials Web Authentication Level 3 (passkeys, security keys) and the Credential Management container it hangs off (navigator.credentials). The options are passed in their standard JSON form (PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptionsJSON / PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptionsJSON: binary members in base64url), which is what a server sends: a module can hand it over as is. The browser checks them, decides the RP ID (a registrable domain suffix of the document's domain), builds clientDataJSON, and asks the operating system's authenticators (Windows: Windows Hello, security keys, a phone), whose dialog the user answers. Only a secure context may call these (SecurityError otherwise); a ceremony needs a recent key press or click in the page (security.webauthn.require_user_activation) and the page's tab shown in the focused window (security.webauthn.require_focus), else NotAllowedError; one ceremony at a time per document. Rejections use the Error codes: Not_Allowed (cancelled, timed out, no credential, refused), Invalid_State (an excluded credential exists), Not_Supported, Security (RP ID), Type (malformed options), Abort (the signal's reason), Encoding (invalid base64url). Module fetch The promise side of the Fetch API, on the same records as the callback API of module net (a Response is a Fetch: Fetch_status, Fetch_headers, Fetch_release... apply to it). Fetch_promise settles with the Response when the headers arrive; it is rejected on a network error (Network) or an abort (the signal's reason). Response_text / Response_arrayBuffer settle when the whole body is there; a body is consumed once (bodyUsed). Response_body is a minimal ReadableStream: Stream_read settles with a buffer of what arrived since the last read, or with 0 (text "done") at the end; Stream_cancel stops the download. Architecture How Wren is put together, and the rules that keep it from breaking as it grows. For the overview, the build and the feature list, see the README. The rules that keep it from breaking at scale One ownership tree. process → tab → navigation → page → (instances, DOM, requests, timers). Everything a page starts is registered in its scope (src/base/scope.odin); closing a tab or navigating is scope_close. Cleanups run newest first, children before parents, so nothing outlives what it points to. Scopes are main-thread only. Handles, never pointers, cross boundaries. Handle = generation << 32 | index, 0 is invalid. A destroyed or recycled slot fails to resolve. Late network events, timers and listener callbacks for dead objects are dropped, not delivered to reused memory. Pool objects never move (chunked), so ^T stays valid until removed. Single UI thread, everything else posts. The network stack's threads, the image decoders, the layout and style threads and the blocking pool only push events and host.post back to the loop; every user-visible callback runs on the loop thread. The DOM and the Wasm instances of a page live on the UI thread (workers have their own store). Mechanism and policy are separate. net moves bytes and never follows a redirect, stores a cookie or sends ambient credentials. fetch decides, per hop, on the UI thread, with the document's

The content blocker Wren blocks advertising, tracking and malware natively: the filter engine (src/adblock) is a portable Odin package, the policy layer (src/blocker) joins it to the loader and the pages, and the interface is native (the shield at the end of the address bar, its panel, and the dashboard about:blocker). Nothing is ever reported anywhere; the lists are downloaded from their own servers, never shipped in the repository (the only list built in is a small one written for Wren). The motivation is performance: a blocked request costs no DNS lookup, no connection, no script to download, parse and run, and its frame or image leaves no empty box. Measurements are at the end. b: Driving Wren with CDP and WebDriver BiDi Wren can be driven by the standard automation tools — Puppeteer, Playwright (connectOverCDP or the BiDi transport), Chrome DevTools, and WebDriver BiDi clients — over a local WebSocket. An adapter translates their messages onto the same command engine wren ctl uses (docs/remote.md): there is one control path, not two. Turning it on The adapter is off by default. t: Crash reports and the symbols of a build
b: Crash reports and the symbols of a build When Wren crashes, src/tools/crashtrace writes <profile>\crashes\crash <date> <time>.txt (the faulting thread's stack) and a minidump beside it (.dmp). A program that ended itself with its session open (ExitProcess or TerminateProcess, whoever called them in the executable) leaves exit <date>.txt with the stack that asked for it. A session that ended with no chance to write one is reported at the next start as unclean exit <date>.txt, which says what is left to know: Windows' Application Error event of that process (a fail-fast), a restart of the machine, or a kill from outside. A crash that wrote its report leaves none, nor does a close ended by the shutdown watchdog (shutdown.log in the profile says what it waited for). What is written and when, for a report to survive what caused it: Every faulting thread waits for the report. A second fault (the threads of a pass reading the same freed block) used to end the process under the writer. The filter runs only if the system's search for a handler walks the stack to the thread's start. On a stack it cannot follow (a return address written over, a jump through a bad pointer) it gives up and ends the process with no handler called. The vectored handler walks the stack the same way first, for every 0xC... code, and reports when the walk stops short. The stack is walked in a copy

t: bigint: arbitrary-precision integers for the JavaScript engine
b: bigint: arbitrary-precision integers for the JavaScript engine src/engine/bigint is the ECMAScript BigInt arithmetic, written natively in Odin. The JavaScript engine used to get this from QuickJS's C running inside WebAssembly; this package replaces it with a native implementation that gives identical numeric results and reads like Odin instead of transcribed C. It is allocation-aware: every operation allocates its result through context.allocator, so the engine injects the realm's allocator and frees results with destroy. No OS dependency — it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32. Representation Sign-magnitude, little-endian u32 limbs, always normalized (no leading zero limb; zero is the empty magnitude with neg = false). This is the natural Odin shape and keeps the arithmetic obvious. The one place the choice shows is the bitwise operators: ECMAScript defines & | ^ ~ and >> as if a BigInt were an infinite two's-complement integer, so those operations convert each operand to its two's-complement limb view over a common width, apply the op, and convert back (bits.odin). import bi "wb:engine/bigint" a := bi.from_i64(1_000_000_007) b, _ := bi.from_string("340282366920938463463374607431768211456", 10) // 2^128 defer bi.destroy(&a) defer bi.destroy(&b) p := bi.mul(a, b); defer bi.destroy(&p) q := bi.div(p, a); defer bi.destroy(&q) // == b s :=

t: datetime (package jsdate): the JavaScript engine's Date
b: datetime (package jsdate): the JavaScript engine's Date src/engine/datetime is the ECMAScript Date calendar and string handling, written natively in Odin (the package is named jsdate so it never collides with core:time/datetime). It is ported from QuickJS-ng and produces the same results as QuickJS over the whole valid range, so Date behaves identically without the C that used to run in WebAssembly. Time values are milliseconds since the Unix epoch as f64, NaN for an invalid Date; the valid range is ±8.64 × 10¹⁵ ms (about ±273 790 years). Fields use the ECMAScript order [year, month(0–11), day(1–31), hour, min, sec, ms, weekday, tz-minutes]. The package is allocation-free and has no OS dependency, so it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32. The one thing it cannot compute on its own — the local time zone offset — is a host callback. The time zone callback import jsdate "wb:engine/datetime" jsdate.timezone_offset_proc = proc "contextless" (time_ms: i64) -> int { return host_get_timezone_offset(time_ms) // minutes west of UTC, i.e. getTimezoneOffset(t) } This is the exact role of js.timezone_offset in the Wren host. When the callback is nil, local time equals UTC, so UTC-only code (and tests) work with no host wired up. Using it // time value -> fields (UTC or local) f, ok := jsdate.get_date_fields(t_ms, is_local = true, force = false) //

Moteur JavaScript — front-end E1 (src/engine/frontend) Le paquet frontend est la moitié « amont » du moteur JavaScript écrit en Odin. Il transforme du source ECMAScript en bytecode QuickJS-ng 0.17, identique octet pour octet à ce que produit JS_WriteObject (BC_VERSION 28, drapeaux JS_WRITE_OBJ_BYTECODE | JS_WRITE_OBJ_STRIP_SOURCE), à deux choix près depuis le round 31 de performance.md : o["x"] est o.x, et return f() reste un appel et un retour (plus de tail_call). L'autre moitié (E2 : valeurs, objets, GC, interpréteur, fonctions natives) relit ce bytecode. Les deux moitiés ne se rencontrent qu'au format de bytecode : opcodes.odin, atoms.odin, serialize.odin. Le paquet compile pour windows_amd64, linux_amd64 et freestanding_wasm32. Toute allocation passe par l'allocateur injecté (une arène libère une compilation entière d'un coup). Aucun appel OS, aucune libc. Il réutilise les paquets feuilles numconv (littéraux numériques) et unicode (ucd, données Unicode 17.0.0). Pourquoi un portage direct du compilateur QuickJS La première version passait par un AST (lexer, parseur, résolveur, émetteur séparés ; voir l'historique git, commit dc13ba87). Elle ne pouvait pas atteindre la parité octet : QuickJS émet en une seule passe pendant le parse, et son bytecode dépend de cet ordre exact. The JIT (src/engine/jsrt/jit.odin) A hot loop of a function, or a hot function without loops of its own, is translated from its bytecode to a WebAssembly function, which the host compiles with Cranelift and attaches to the engine's table (src/js/jit.odin, wasm.attach_function); the interpreter then calls it like a C function pointer. WebAssembly stays the only execution engine: the code made at run time lives in the engine's sandbox and reaches only the engine's memory, its table and the helpers the engine exports to it. When a loop is compiled The interpreter's hot loop counts back edges for the interrupt poll; every INTERRUPT_POLL_EVERY of them it leaves to the full dispatch, which offers the back edge to jit_back_edge. A check falls on a loop in proportion to the part it has in what runs: a loop met by javascript.jit.loop_threshold of them (Jit_Loop.sightings) is hot, one met once is not: compiled at its first sighting, theverge.com translated 1 600 loops during its load for nothing it got back. It is then translated (jit_build) and entered at its header (on-stack replacement), with the frame's arguments, locals and operand stack in memory. While a loop of a function is compiled, the hot loop leaves at that loop's back edges only (jit_loop_taken); the function's other loops stay in it. t: numconv: float64 ↔ string for the JavaScript engine
b: numconv: float64 ↔ string for the JavaScript engine src/engine/numconv is the part of the JavaScript engine that turns a float64 into the string a script sees (String(x), Number.prototype.toString/toFixed/toExponential/toPrecision) and parses a string back into a float64 (Number(s), parseFloat, parseInt). It is written natively in Odin, ported deliberately from QuickJS-ng's dtoa.c (Fabrice Bellard, MIT), and produces the same bytes as QuickJS for every finite f64 and every radix 2–36, so the engine's number output never depends on the C that used to run inside WebAssembly. It is allocation-free: the string producers write into a caller buffer and return the length, the parsers read a string, and the bignum scratch that the algorithm needs lives on fixed stack arrays (what QuickJS kept in JSDTOATempMem/JSATODTempMem). That is what lets the package build for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with no allocator and no OS. Using it import nc "wb:engine/numconv" buf: [nc.MAX_STR_LEN]u8 // always big enough for any dtoa output n := nc.f64_to_shortest(buf[:], 3.14) // "3.14" (String(x), base 10) n = nc.f64_to_radix(buf[:], 255, 16) // "ff" (Number.prototype.toString(16)) n = nc.f64_to_fixed(buf[:], 1.5, 3) // "1.500" (toFixed(3)) n = nc.f64_to_exponential(buf[:], 12345, 2) // "1.23e+4" (toExponential(2)) n = nc.f64_to_precision(buf[:], 12345, 3) // "1.23e+4"

engine/regexp Odin port of QuickJS-ng's libregexp: a full ECMAScript regular-expression parser and bytecode compiler, plus a bounded backtracking interpreter. It replaces the C engine and leans on the language — tagged opcodes, interval character sets, caller-supplied allocators, an explicit (non-recursive) backtrack stack — so it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with no libc. The browser uses it for URLPattern (src/url/pattern_match.odin: a component's regular expression, with the v flag). import rx "wb:engine/regexp" API re, err := rx.compile(pattern, flags, allocator) // flags: rx.Flags bit_set defer rx.destroy(&re) if err.message != "" { /* compile error at err.pos */ } caps: rx.Captures st := rx.exec_search(&re, rx.input_utf16(units), start, &caps, limits, allocator) // st is .Match / .No_Match / .Out_Of_Steps / .Stack_Overflow if st == .Match { whole := caps.groups[0] // {start, end} in code-unit offsets, or {-1,-1} if unset idx, ok := rx.named_group_index(&re, "year") } Flags d g i m s u v y — rx.parse_flags("gims") → rx.Flags; rx.flags_to_string. Input is a slice of code units, either UTF-16 (rx.input_utf16, JS semantics, offsets are UTF-16 indices) or UTF-8 (rx.input_utf8 / rx.input_utf8_string, offsets are byte indices). Surrogate pairs combine only in unicode mode. exec tries exactly one start offset; exec_search scans forward

The ECMAScript runtime (src/engine/jsrt) The runtime is the "second half" of Wren's Odin JavaScript engine: it executes QuickJS‑ng 0.17 bytecode. It is written natively in Odin, builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with an injected allocator and no OS dependency, and runs inside Wren's Wasm sandbox exactly as QuickJS‑in‑Wasm does (the sandbox is kept on purpose: it protects the host from memory bugs of the engine). The two halves of the engine meet at the QuickJS‑ng 0.17 bytecode: the Odin front‑end (frontend.md) and the reference QuickJS C compiler emit the same serialized form, and this runtime reads and runs it. compile_frontend.odin calls the front‑end in process (a scratch arena per compile), so eval, Function(...), modules and $262.evalScript need no other compiler. This is not a mechanical port of QuickJS. Where the C uses #define tags, manual refcounting and hand‑rolled dispatch, the Odin version uses tagged unions with exhaustive switch, defer, arenas where they help, comptime‑generated opcode/atom tables, and layouts friendly to #soa. Divergences are deliberate and listed at the end. Conformance (test262) wrentool engine test262 builds the judge (src/engine/jsrt/judge) and runs the suite pinned by src/tools/test262 in worker processes (a crash or hang costs one test), with the rules of QuickJS‑ng's test262.conf. engine/unicode (ucd) Odin port of QuickJS-ng's libunicode. It provides the Unicode data the regexp engine and the JS lexer need: character-set intervals, case conversion / folding / the ECMAScript regexp canonicalize, the identifier and whitespace predicates, the \p{} property / general-category / script sets, and the four normalization forms. The package is named ucd (not unicode) so it does not collide with core:unicode. Import it with an alias: import ucd "wb:engine/unicode" It compiles for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32. Nothing in the runtime path touches the OS; every allocation goes through a caller-supplied allocator (pass an arena to free a whole build at once). t: The DOM of a same-origin frame
b: The DOM of a same-origin frame Each document has its own JavaScript realm: an instance of the engine, compiled to Wasm, with its own heap. A browser's frames share a heap between documents of one origin, and pages rely on it: iframe.contentDocument.write(html), frame.contentWindow.someGlobal, parent.document, window.parent.foo(), rich-text editors, payment widgets, test harnesses. Wren gets the same result without sharing a heap, in two parts. Nodes: handles that name their document The DOM lives on the browser's side; a wrapper in a realm is a handle. A handle now says which document it belongs to: 15 bits of its generation word are the document's tag (base.pool_insert_tagged, src/base/pool.odin). So a wrapper of a realm can hold a node of another document, and contentDocument and all that is reached from it are ordinary DOM wrappers of the caller's realm. Every generated import trampoline hands its handle arguments to api_route (src/page/api_host.odin). A handle of another document moves the whole call to that document: Call.page is that page, Call.caller the one whose realm is calling, and the implementation does what it does for a page calling itself, so the frame's styles, layout, hooks and scripts follow. Imports of Document that name no node (createTextNode, title, write...) are preceded by a one-shot Frame_target. What keeps a frame of another origin out: a handle

t: Translating Wren: how the texts are written
b: Translating Wren: how the texts are written Every text the user reads goes through the i18n package (src/i18n), so that a language can be added without going through the code again. Today English is the only language and tr returns its argument: writing the texts the right way now is what makes the translation cheap later. The plan and the open questions are in the maintainer's notes ("Internationalisation"). import "wb:i18n" label := i18n.tr("Open in a new tab") close := i18n.tr("tab strip", "Close") // a context for the translator, never shown text := fmt.tprintf(i18n.tr(count, "%d request", "%d requests"), count) // singular, plural, by count One name, tr, a procedure group: the compiler picks the form from the arguments (a text; a context and a text; a count and two forms). The English text is the key: no identifier to invent, and the code reads as before. English only, and no cost English is the only language for now, and the package has no code to load another one yet. tr returns its argument, a string literal in the executable's read-only data: no lookup, no allocation, no copy, and the texts stay side by side where the linker put them. A test (english_returns_the_same_bytes) keeps it that way. A language, when there is one, must not cost more than that, because the interface is drawn every frame and tr runs for every label: One blob, not many strings. The translations

Wren documentation Wren is a web browser written from scratch in Odin, for Windows, where WebAssembly is the only execution engine — JavaScript included. The scripts of a page run in an engine written in Odin and compiled to WebAssembly, inside the same Wasmtime sandbox, memory cap and interruption as every other module. The web platform itself (DOM, CSS, layout, painting, Fetch, the shell) is native Odin, drawn on Direct3D 11. There is no Chromium underneath. A page can also be a single .wasm file that calls the browser directly, through imports generated from Web IDL: see Web API. Installing Wren is a single executable for Windows x64. There is no installer to run as administrator: Download the latest wren-<version>-windows-x64.exe from the releases page and run it: the program is that one file, with nothing to unzip. wren.exe --setup installs it. Or, for a release that has reached winget: winget install FromentSoftware.Wren. Every version is free during the beta. A Wren User License unlocks nothing during the beta; it keeps the work going and covers two years of updates from 1.0. Driving Wren You rarely need to click to test a page. b: Writing Wren's JavaScript glue in Odin Wren's JavaScript engine is the Odin engine (src/engine/jsrt, through the QuickJS C API of src/engine/jscapi) compiled to one WebAssembly module (build/js/wren_js.wasm), run by Wasmtime. Around the engine sits the glue: the code that implements the web platform's objects as native functions of that API and wires them to the browser's wr_* imports. All of it is Odin (native/js/odin/; the binding tables are generated into bindings_gen.odin). No C of ours is compiled any more: the module is linked by the wasm-ld that ships with Odin, with no C library (wj/libc.odin). This document is the rule book: where things go, how to declare them, how to add a domain. The generic ABI that will replace the hand-written transmission layer is in odin-abi.md. Web Audio AudioContext, OfflineAudioContext, their nodes and decodeAudioData. What a script sees is JavaScript (native/js/odin/web_audio.js, evaluated the first time a realm of a window reads one of the interfaces: a page that never asks pays nothing). The graph, its threads and every computation are the browser's: src/webaudio, a package with no JavaScript in it and its own unit tests. src/page/bindings_webaudio.odin and api/webaudio.widl are between the two. The render graph A node is a number of a graph; a graph is a host object of the page. The page's thread and the render thread share the graph under one lock, which the render thread holds for one quantum (128 frames) at a time. A running AudioContext has one thread and one media.Audio_Output (backend_audio_output: WASAPI on Windows, cpal on Linux, the null output with WREN_AUDIO_OUTPUT=null or no device). The thread keeps the output's queue at the latency asked for, a quantum at a time: the device's clock paces the rendering, and so currentTime. Suspending ends the thread and closes the stream. An OfflineAudioContext has a thread until its rendering is over, as fast as it goes. suspend(t) stops it at a quantum (rounded up) until resume(). The order of processing is recomputed when connections change: every node runs, a source with nowhere to go still ends and an analyser still listens. A cycle goes through a DelayNode

Wren User Licenses Wren is a beta under development and every version is free. During the beta a supporter license only supports its development: it unlocks nothing, nothing in Wren checks it, and no window or reminder asks for one. Once Wren is out of beta, the updates that follow need a license, and one bought during the beta covers them. The only visible effect is one line of about:wren: without a license: Unregistered — free during the beta · Support Wren; with one: Registered to <name>, with the edition, the date, the order number and a thank-you. The code is under the PolyForm Strict License 1.0.0 (LICENSE). A supporter license is separate from the code's license. How it works A license is a statement signed offline with an Ed25519 private key that only the maintainer has. Wren holds the matching public key and checks the signature on the user's computer, without any network access (core:crypto/ed25519, package src/license). No server is involved in checking. Issuing is either manual (the maintainer signs a license with wrentool license and sends it) or automatic: licenses are sold through Paddle (the seller of record, who handles VAT), and a small Cloudflare Worker (licence/worker, free plan) signs the license when Paddle reports a paid transaction, keeps it, mails it, and shows it on the thank-you page. Both produce byte-identical licenses; see Selling with Paddle.

Artistic new tab When browser.newtab.art.enabled is on, a new tab shows a random public-domain painting filling the window, with the start page's shortcuts and the address bar legible over it, a discreet caption (title, artist, date, museum, a link to the record) and two small buttons (Another painting, Open the record). It follows Google Arts Culture's "art new tab" idea, but every piece runs natively in Wren: the engine renders the page, the shell downloads and caches the images. The option is off by default. When the network is touched Never while the option is off, and never while the loader is held offline. With the option on, the paintings an earlier session kept and nobody saw yet are taken back at the start, without the network, so the first new tab has one at once. A background task then starts about 2.5 seconds after the start (or after the option is turned on), so that a first session has one too; it also starts at the first art new tab if it was stopped. Until a painting is ready, the new tab shows a gradient with a spinner and "Fetching a painting…", and is replaced by the painting as soon as one is. From then on the task keeps a sliding window of about browser.newtab.art.window paintings ready, downloading a fresh one whenever a shown painting is consumed. Performance: the pipelines measured Wren seen as a factory: each stage of a pipeline produces at some rate and consumes at another, and the slowest stage, or a queue that holds what a stage made, sets the throughput. This page has the map with numbers, the bottleneck of each pipeline, an inventory of what goes against the rules below, and what to do next, ranked. The rules the work follows: data laid out for the loops that read it (struct of arrays where a loop reads a few fields of many items, flat arrays rather than hash tables, indices rather than pointers); no cache to hide a slow path (the caches that are a product, the HTTP cache, the back/forward cache, compiled code on disk, stay); lists with an inline capacity rather than heap lists; bitsets rather than arrays of bools; no mutex where an ownership hand-off, per-thread state, an SPSC ring or an MPSC queue does; explicit state machines in structures. How it was measured On the development machine (2026-11-02), headless (api.Window_Mode.Headless: no window, nothing takes the focus), the profile build (build.bat profile, -define:PROFILE=true) with the native library of the development builds (Cargo quick: text shaping 2 to 5 % slower than the shipped one, see native/Cargo.toml). Tools: wrentool bench perf -Only <scenario>: start to load, frames, CPU, memory, and the browser's own report per scenario

Wren 0.3.0 Wren 0.3.0 compiles JavaScript to WebAssembly, loads iframes and no longer lets a busy page freeze the browser. Hot functions and loops of QuickJS-ng are compiled to Wasm modules on background threads, then by Wasmtime (Cranelift); guards fall back to the interpreter exactly. Highlights A search box on the start page. It does what the address bar does with the same text: words go to the default search engine (a keyword such as @g cats picks another), an address opens as it is. The small texts at the bottom of the page are gone; the version and "by Froment Software" stay. Suggestions on focus. A click in the address bar, Ctrl+L or a new tab lists the pages visited most and most lately before anything is typed. Nothing is chosen at first, so Enter still does what the field says. browser.urlbar.top_sites turns it off. Fixed A visited page no longer takes the title "New tab" (or an error page's title) in the history and in the suggestions.

Wren 0.6.12 Wren 0.6.12 slows middle-click autoscroll down by half and brings the first painting sooner. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Middle-click autoscroll is half as fast: the top speed is 15000 px/s (was 30000), reached at the same distance; every speed in between is halved. browser.scroll.autoscroll.max_speed sets it. The first painting comes sooner. With nothing downloaded yet, the smallest of the listed files goes first, and a file larger than browser.newtab.art.max_image_bytes is no longer downloaded just to fail. The page reads "Loading a painting…" instead of "No painting could be loaded yet". Changed The icons of the start page's search box (the lens and the arrow) are bigger.

Wren 0.6.13 Wren 0.6.13 adds a download manager. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights A downloads button and its drop-down. Once a download has run, a button joins the toolbar: a ring fills around its arrow as the files arrive, and the drop-down (it opens by itself when a download begins) lists the latest ones with a progress bar, the speed and the time left. The cross cancels, a click opens the file, the folder icon shows it in the file manager. about:downloads (Ctrl+J). Every download by day, with a search box. Per file: Open, Show in folder, Copy download link, Download again, Delete the file, Remove from the list; Try again for a failed one; Clear the list for all the finished ones. A list that stays. The finished downloads are kept across restarts (up to browser.download.list_max, 200 by default); a file moved or deleted since says so. A progress bar that is good to look at: it eases toward the real figure, with a gloss on its upper half and a light band travelling over it; a comet runs while the size is not announced.

Wren 0.6.14 Wren 0.6.14 sends the downloads straight to a folder you choose. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights No Save dialog by default. browser.download.ask is now off: a file goes at once to the download folder, under a name that is free (the Downloads folder of Windows unless you chose another). The folder is yours to choose. At the top of about:downloads, the folder in use with Change… (the folder picker of Windows) and Default (back to the Downloads folder of Windows), and a switch "Ask where to save each file" for those who prefer the Save dialog.

Wren 0.6.15 Wren 0.6.15 styles big pages several times faster. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights A style pass that really uses the threads. On a page whose elements sit under one chain of containers (GitHub, most web apps), the work was shared level by level, so one thread did nearly all of it. It is now shared by weight. A full pass on the Wren repository page on GitHub goes from about 190 ms to 52 ms; its styles take 1.5 s instead of 3.6 s while it loads, and the 95th percentile of the gaps between two frames goes from 480 to 330 ms. A way to measure a real site: tools\perf.ps1 -Only github_load,github_scroll loads and scrolls the repository page with the profiler.

Wren 0.6.16 Wren 0.6.16 loads pages made of ES modules faster: GitHub, and most modern sites. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Each module is compiled once. The engine compiled every ES module twice: when it arrived, to learn what it imports, and again when the graph ran, because the first was not kept. It is now kept. Modules are in the bytecode cache. Compiled modules go to the profile's cache, as classic scripts already did, so a module seen before is read instead of parsed. On the repository page of Wren on GitHub (about 130 modules) the page is stable after 4.0 s instead of 7.8 s on a visit that finds them in the cache, and the longest stall between two frames goes from 1.9 s to 0.7 s. The first visit gains about a second.

Wren 0.6.17 Wren 0.6.17 stops stuttering when the pointer moves over a page like GitHub's. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Hovering no longer restyles the page. On GitHub's repository page, every move of the pointer over a link or a topic tag made a full style pass, about 120 ms each, so the page drew four frames a second under the pointer. Two rules were the cause: a :has() with a hover inside it, and an :is() with a state in it, which the partial restyle took for a match everywhere. Both are now scoped: a state change costs 1.3 ms of style work on average instead of 29 ms, and the share of frames over their budget while the pointer moves falls from 40 % to 4 %. Large ES modules are compiled off the interface thread, like large classic scripts: the page does its other work while a compile thread makes the bytecode.

Wren 0.6.18 Wren 0.6.18 fixes a use of freed memory that Linux revealed, and brings the Linux build to the point where it runs. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only: the Linux build is not released yet. Highlights performance.getEntriesByType("navigation") read freed memory. The strings of the navigation entry were freed before they were turned into JSON. The Windows heap left them in place, so nothing showed; on Linux they were overwritten, and GitHub's web-vitals code failed with JSON.parse: bad escape, which left its repository page on "Unable to load page". Fixed. JSON.parse errors say where they stopped, with the text around the position. Wren links and runs on Linux (checked under WSLg on NixOS): the window, the start page, wren ctl, and GitHub's repository page. Nothing to download yet: ./build.sh deps and ./build.sh wren build it, and docs/portability.md lists what was checked and what was not. A new tab no longer puts the keyboard in the address bar (browser.newtab.focus_address brings it back): Ctrl+T opens the new tab page, and the list of frequent pages does not drop over it. The latest gui_toolkit.

Wren 0.6.19 Wren 0.6.19 stops GitHub's file list from running over its sidebar, and answers input a frame sooner. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights table-layout: fixed is honoured. A table with a width and table-layout: fixed took its columns from the content, so a commit message that does not wrap widened the file list of a GitHub repository page over its sidebar. The columns now come from the <col> elements and the first row, and the automatic ones share what is left. A frame less between input and screen, from the latest gui_toolkit: on GitHub, with the pointer moving over the page, the time from an input to the refresh that shows it goes from 49.9 ms to 35.9 ms on average (60 Hz screen, same machine and page). The toolkit also gains a lazy column, ui.next_merge, ui.box_at and layout warnings in debug builds.

Wren 0.6.2 Wren 0.6.2 links its JavaScript engine with no Zig and no C library, and repairs its documentation site. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights No Zig, no C library. The engine module is linked by the wasm-ld that ships with Odin. The heap, the string functions, strtod, snprintf and ldexp are Odin (native/js/odin/wj/libc.odin), exp is fdlibm's, and sin, cos and pow come from the host. Only Lexbor remains as external C. The documentation site. Its pages use links relative to the site's root, so they have their style, logo and search under /wren/. Code wraps instead of overflowing. The changelog page and the version on the home page follow the releases. The pictures of the home page. Four pictures of one window with four tabs, as the clickable zones expect, and new captures of every page from a current build.

Wren 0.6.20 Wren 0.6.20 runs a page's own WebAssembly: Blazor, Rust and Emscripten applications now start. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights The WebAssembly JavaScript API. WebAssembly.compile, instantiate, the streaming forms, Module, Instance, Memory, Table, Global, Tag and Exception, in windows and workers. A .NET 10 Blazor application that said "This browser does not support WebAssembly" now works, first through its server circuit, then with .NET itself in WebAssembly; a Yew (Rust) application and SQLite Fiddle (Emscripten) start too. On web-platform-tests wasm/jsapi, 82 % of the subtests pass. A large module does not stop the page. WebAssembly.compile works on another thread: for a 34 MB module, the page's timers keep running (worst gap 25 ms) where a synchronous compile blocks for 440 ms. A page that does not touch WebAssembly pays nothing: its objects are made on first use. The page's Content Security Policy applies ('wasm-unsafe-eval'). Limits A script reading a module's memory element by element is slow (186 ns per read, against 15 ns for an ordinary array): the memory is reached through the browser. The module itself runs at Wasmtime's speed, and bulk operations (set, slice, TextDecoder) are one call. No shared memory, so no WebAssembly threads. Modules using the old form of exceptions (older Emscripten and .NET builds) do not

Wren 0.6.21 Wren 0.6.21 runs far more of the web's WebAssembly, and starts it faster: DuckDB, Python and older .NET and C++ builds. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Modules built with the old form of WebAssembly exceptions run. try, catch, rethrow and delegate are what older Emscripten and .NET builds use, and Wasmtime refuses them: they are now translated at compilation. DuckDB's shell (3.8 MB of C++) starts. Python runs. new WebAssembly.Memory({shared: true}) works for one agent, as other browsers allow without isolation, so Pyodide starts and answers runPython. Faster. A script going through a module's memory one element at a time is 3 to 4 times faster, and an instance with thousands of exports takes 104 ms instead of 5.7 s: Pyodide starts in 5.7 s instead of 11.5 s. A module can catch what JavaScript throws (catch_all, WebAssembly.JSTag), a call can have any number of values, and externrefs are released once the module has dropped them. Service workers: event.waitUntil() works from the promise given to respondWith, as the specification allows. bitplatform.dev's Blazor application starts. Streams: releasing a reader during a read no longer reports an unhandled rejection, which stopped DuckDB's worker and failed pipeTo tests. Changes you may notice Without cross-origin isolation a page has no global SharedArrayBuffer, as in other

Wren 0.6.22 Wren 0.6.22 comes to Linux, runs WebAssembly threads and a real crypto.subtle, and stays far smoother on pages that change every frame. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights A Linux package. wren-0.6.22-linux-x64.tar.gz for x86-64, an early preview: it needs glibc 2.39 or later (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 40). It is built and started on a clean machine before it is published. Keyboard, pointer and a real GPU on Linux were not checked for this release. WebAssembly threads and SharedArrayBuffer under cross-origin isolation. Squoosh encodes an image in a worker. A real crypto.subtle: AES, HMAC, PBKDF2, HKDF, ECDSA and ECDH on P-256 and P-384, RSA, Ed25519 and X25519, in pages and workers. amazon.com renders. P-521 is not there yet. Much smoother with a UI Automation program around. A screenshot tool or PowerToys kept a page's accessibility tree updating on every frame. It now updates ten times a second at most: resizing a 10 000-item flex page went from 6.9 to about 28 frames a second, and a page of 10 000 changing nodes from 1.9 to about 8. A value lost by the garbage collector. What an async function returned could be collected before its promise took it: an ArrayBuffer turned up empty, a rejection reason undefined. More of the web works: blob: URLs for every load, link preload, the common SVG DOM, FontFace, real CSSRule objects, a document for

Wren 0.6.23 Wren 0.6.23 plays Web Audio, and vscode.dev, tldraw and reddit work. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Web Audio. AudioContext, OfflineAudioContext, the usual nodes, decodeAudioData and ScriptProcessorNode, on Windows and Linux, following the autoplay policy. The web-platform-tests of webaudio go from 24 % to 92 %. AudioWorklet is not there yet. vscode.dev works: its compile no longer runs into a time limit, large scripts compile about 3.6 times faster, a service worker's opaque answer reaches the page, and a <meta> policy no longer applies to code before it. reddit works: a form submitted while the page loads goes through, a hang that grew to 22 GB of memory is gone, and getComputedStyle answers for shorthands. tldraw's icons show: an SVG image's fragment now makes :target match. Regular expressions search faster: Octane's regexp from 127 to about 165. A same-origin frame gives navigator, screen and crypto, which scripts often take from a frame they just made.

Wren 0.6.24 Wren 0.6.24 draws WebGL and positions with CSS anchors: Three.js and MapLibre run. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights WebGL and WebGL 2, through wgpu and naga, with a device and a thread for each context. Three.js examples and MapLibre maps run: a simple scene at 60 frames a second, a heavy one at 20 to 30, on a good GPU. A machine with no adapter gets null, as a page expects. Transform feedback and real queries are not there yet, nor WebGL in workers. There is no separate GPU process: a crash inside a driver takes the browser down. CSS anchor positioning: anchor(), anchor-size(), position-area, position-try-fallbacks, @position-try, position-visibility, implicit anchors of popovers. The web-platform-tests of the folder go from 13.7 % to 85 %. No writing modes or anchor names across shadow trees. A compiled loop's return no longer leaks stack depth: pages could end in a false "Maximum call stack". TypedArray.prototype.set no longer traps on large arrays. Scroll containers count the end margins of their children as scrollable overflow, as other browsers do: scrollHeight may grow.

Wren 0.6.25 Wren 0.6.25 opens the DOM of same-origin frames, lays out columns and vertical text, and sleeps when nothing changes. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Same-origin frames: contentDocument, contentWindow.document, parent.document; each frame keeps its own built-ins (instanceof across frames is false, as in other browsers); a frame's navigations fire their navigate event and keep their own session history. Multi-column layout and vertical writing modes: columns, column-span, nested columns, writing-mode, text-orientation, and documents that scroll horizontally or start from the bottom. A GPU process for WebGL, WebGL in workers and transferControlToOffscreen, WebGL 2 transform feedback and queries. AudioWorklet, and P-521 in crypto.subtle. Pages that build large documents run about three times faster: identical styles shared, columns laid out on the layout threads, wrappers of plain nodes freed without the cost of a full collection (a page that rebuilds 10 000 nodes every frame, measured on one machine: about 28 - 85 frames a second). An image opened by itself is a viewer: zoom around the pointer (Ctrl+wheel, pinch, + and -), drag to pan, R to turn it, a click between fitted and 100 %. A browser at rest draws nothing: no frame and almost no wake on a page that changes nothing, and a caret that blinks redraws only its own pixels. Faster and safer

Wren 0.6.26 Wren 0.6.26 runs pages that build large documents again much faster, and reads pages written in legacy encodings right. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Pages that rebuild their DOM are much faster: elements alike share their selector matching, document and window stay on the interpreter's fast path, a wrapper is one allocation, string arguments are read in place and a collection unpins its nodes in one call (a page that rebuilds 10 000 nodes every frame, measured on one machine: about 85 - 142 frames a second since 0.6.25). Legacy encodings: a page in Shift_JIS, EUC-KR, Big5, GBK or windows-1252 keeps its encoding for its links and forms (a search form no longer sends mojibake), document.characterSet says it, level-2 kanji decode, and documents made by a script keep their own encoding and URL. getComputedStyle gives the used insets (top, right, bottom, left in pixels) of positioned elements: what tooltip and popover libraries read. <dialog>: beforetoggle and toggle events, closedBy, and a modal dialog leaves the top layer when it is taken out of the document. document.createProcessingInstruction, and an error of a method of another frame's node is of that frame. Text on several threads waits less (the graphics toolkit's atlas and word cache locks).

Wren 0.6.27 Wren 0.6.27 fixes links that all showed their hover style together, and follows the standards more closely for names, international domain names and forms. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Hovering one link no longer restyles its look-alikes: links that share a style (a site's nav, the start page's Configuration, History and Content blocker links) each show their hover state alone again. International domain names follow the URL Standard: xn-- hosts are only lowercased, labels starting with a combining mark or with a misplaced zero-width joiner are refused. Names as scripts give them: createElementNS and setAttributeNS keep their case, namespace selectors (*|div, |div) work, and an iframe answered as XML is shown as an XML document. Two forms sent at once to two frames both arrive (the second used to cancel the first). A setTimeout(0) set by a script runs after the tasks that script queued, as in other browsers. XHR and FileReader text honour a byte order mark. Full style passes are faster again (the page's color scheme read from its <meta> elements, subtrees weighed in one walk), and pages with columns build their display list on the layout threads.

Wren 0.6.28 Wren 0.6.28 gives its scroll bars room as Chrome's, docks its developer tools, keeps frames and popups in the history, and runs pages that rebuild their DOM faster again. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Classic scroll bars: page and element scroll bars take their room, with arrows at their ends (documentElement.clientWidth is the window less the bar, as in Chrome on Windows); scrollbar-gutter and scrollbar-width apply. The old overlay bars are layout.scrollbar.overlay. Developer tools you dock: drag a tab onto a panel or an edge to split, onto a strip to join it, out to float it; panes resize from a few em to nearly the whole room and fold; the layout is kept in the profile. History through frames: back and forward walk the navigations made inside frames, a frame keeps the Window of its first blank document, and so does a window opened by window.open; anchor links and back within a page scroll as the HTML standard says; scroll anchoring keeps the view when content loads above it. Faster pages that rebuild their DOM: one call into the browser makes a node, the collection skips wrappers that hold nothing, the interpreter calls getters itself (a page that rebuilds 10,000 nodes every frame, measured on one machine: about 142 - 163 frames a second). More of the web platform: ::backdrop, ::placeholder, scrollend, document.domain, CSP Embedded

Wren 0.6.29 Wren 0.6.29 can install its own updates, signed and checked, and brings devtools, JIT and compatibility work. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Signed updates (Windows): a release carries a manifest signed with a key of its own. About Wren checks for a newer release and, when you press "Install the update", downloads the program, compares its length and SHA-256 with the signed ones, and swaps it in with a way back. Nothing is installed without the button. The channel (address, files, key, signature required) is configurable: see docs/updates.md. Developer tools: find in the panels, a console drawer, a colour picker, style values. Faster scripts: the JIT compiles whole functions, calls, objects, strings and DOM getters. Compatibility: SVG foreignObject, CSS module scripts, subresource integrity, script preparation, CSSOM rules and innerText, among many fixes (see the list below). Help: the licence help button opens a GitHub issue form with your order number filled in.

Wren 0.6.3 Wren 0.6.3 repairs tabs and scrolling, and lays out Bootstrap's documentation as the other browsers do. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Tabs. A middle click on a tab closes it again. A tab dragged onto another window's tabs shows where it would go: the carried window steps aside, the tabs make room and a faded copy of the tab stands in the gap. Scrolling while a page is busy. The page's scroll bar no longer jumps up and down while a script keeps the interface thread: it was drawn into the kept picture of the page and moved with it. The loading bar and the page held during a navigation are the same in every frame. Bootstrap's documentation. A grid item with a stated minimum no longer stretches the flexible tracks (the content column of its pages), <meta http-equiv="refresh"> redirects work, and a script that writes a style it already has no longer restyles the page: its table of contents did it at every scroll event. The tab sidebar. A light line along its inner edge shows where the page begins, in both styles.

Wren 0.6.30 Wren 0.6.30 fixes a crash on pages with radio buttons, keeps animations and scrolling alive under busy scripts, and puts a new tab's keyboard in the address bar. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights A crash fixed: styling a page with radio buttons on several threads could free a list twice and abort Wren (seen on Linux on Wikipedia). The style threads now only read the forms' state, settled before they start. A busy page keeps moving: while a page's script runs a long task, CSS animations of transform and opacity go on, scroll boxes follow the wheel and their scroll bar, and the caret keeps blinking. New tab: Ctrl+T puts the keyboard in the address bar; the list of pages visited opens for a click or a letter, not by itself. With the art new tab on, the first painting is fetched a moment after the start. Compatibility: CSS Nesting's nested declarations, document.write's insertion point, promise rejections and muted errors as HTML reports them, toggle on <details>, clicks dispatched by scripts.

Wren 0.6.31 Wren 0.6.31 is much faster on heavy pages: first paint comes up to three times sooner, loads take about a third less time, and the first page after an install no longer waits for the JavaScript engine to compile. This is still a beta, under development. It also holds everything prepared for 0.6.30, which was never published. Highlights First paint: a web font on its way no longer holds the whole page back, and long scripts leave room for the first frame. Measured from a first load: cnn.com about 1.6 s down to 0.5 s, theverge.com 0.75 s to 0.45 s, bbc.com 1.1 s to about 0.2 s. Loads: a faster JavaScript engine and far fewer full style passes. cnn.com from about 6.3 s to 3.5 s; Wren is still 2 to 4 times slower than Edge on these heavy pages. First page after an install or an update: the engine's machine code now ships in the program, instead of being compiled on the first script. On cnn.com, first paint goes from 3.3 s to 0.6 s on a new profile, and from 17.7 s to 0.75 s on two cores. The program is about 22 MB larger for it. Busy pages: selection, scroll bars, the caret and CSS animations keep working while a script holds the page, and scripts can be interrupted inside the engine's own loops. Fixes: YouTube search finishes again, Ctrl+T gives the keyboard to the address bar, triple click selects reliably, scroll bars answer the pointer, and a page no longer blinks

Wren 0.6.32 Wren 0.6.32 makes the browser's own behaviour steadier: what happens to a press, a key, a navigation and a loading page is now decided in one place each, which removes a long list of bugs. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Navigation: Escape before a page answers no longer leaves a dead tab, a document unloads once, and a page you have left no longer writes into the next page's history entry. Mouse: one owner for the pressed button. A press no longer survives a navigation or a tab switch, Escape during a drag really ends it, and a scroll bar's arrow held across a tab switch no longer keeps the browser busy. Keyboard and address bar: letters no longer go to a frame of a hidden tab, what you are typing in the address bar stays, Ctrl+L works in full screen with the bars hidden. Busy pages: input held under a long script no longer lands on another tab or window, and every window keeps its picture of the page, so a page does not show its background alone. Page loads: deferred scripts and modules wait for the first paint, and cnn.com loads about a fifth faster with less style work. Crash recovery: its files are written again when another program holds them open, as a virus scanner can.

Wren 0.6.4 Wren 0.6.4 keeps fixed headers in place while a page is busy, and removes a feature that never ran. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Fixed and sticky boxes while a page is busy. When a script keeps the interface thread and the wheel scrolls the kept picture of the page, a fixed header or a sticky box (Bootstrap's documentation header) stays where the page drew it, instead of sliding with the picture and jumping back. No more partial redraw. browser.gpu.partial_redraw never ran on a window; the compositor no longer hashes every chunk at every frame for it. setAttribute with the same value changes nothing in the document: observers still see the write, but there is no restyle and no layout. Tests. The end-to-end sessions that drive a Wren run on a developer's machine, not on the shared runner; the release workflow no longer runs the tests again.

Wren 0.6.5 Wren 0.6.5 makes drags work in frames, and sends the pointer's events where other browsers do. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Drags in frames. An iframe's scripts now get mousemove / pointermove and the boundary events, and a document in which a button was pressed keeps the moves while it is held. jQuery UI's demos (draggable, droppable, sortable, resizable, selectable, slider) work in their frames. The pointer over an empty part of a page is over the root element: mousedown, mousemove, mouseup and click reach it, as do :hover. A script that waited for a mouseup over the background no longer believes the button is still down. Order of the pointer's events. The move comes before the press or release that follows it in the same frame. Autoscroll (middle click): the speed grows geometrically with the distance from the anchor, max * (2^(x/D) - 1) / (2^(F/D) - 1), and doubles every 80 px by default (browser.scroll.autoscroll.doubling_distance). Images in shrink-to-fit boxes (blog.jquery.com): an image with a percentage max-width no longer makes its inline-block link as wide as itself.

Wren 0.6.6 Wren 0.6.6 keeps a sticky header at the top while a page is busy, scrolls much faster with the middle click, and records timelines of its frames. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights A sticky header stays at the top while the wheel scrolls the kept picture of a page that a script keeps busy: it was drawn once, lower, and not at its place for the frames made meanwhile (Bootstrap's documentation). wren ctl timeline records every frame the renderer draws, chrome frames included, and writes them as pictures with a contact sheet and a JSON of what each frame was. It is how the header above was found. Middle-click autoscroll is much faster: up to 30000 px/s, reached 300 px from the anchor, the speed doubling every 60 px. The cursor over an iframe is its document's: jQuery UI's resize handles show the resize cursor.

Wren 0.6.7 Wren 0.6.7 updates its toolkit and corrects its README. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights gui_toolkit at its latest master: a Linux window with its platform services, password fields, fuzzy_score, check boxes and switches that fit their mark and label. The README no longer opens with the toolkit's old description and describes the JavaScript engine as the one written in Odin.

Wren 0.6.8 Wren 0.6.8 exports the frames it draws from its developer tools. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights Performance tab: Pictures and Export. Pictures records the window's frames as pictures; Export writes a folder to the downloads folder: a page (index.html) that shows the frames big, one at a time or in a strip, with how much each changed and its time, kind, scroll and difference from the one before; the pictures and a contact sheet; timeline.json; and trace.json, the phases of every frame as Chrome trace events (the Performance tab of Chrome and Perfetto open it). wren ctl timeline stop writes the same index.html.

Wren 0.6.9 Wren 0.6.9 puts the painting start page one click away, and fixes its first appearance. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights A switch on the pages themselves. The start page has a card, "A painting on every new tab", that turns the painting start page on; the painting page has a "Plain start page" link that turns it off. No more digging in the settings. Only the address bar or a link of the start page itself can flip it: a web page cannot. The first painting arrives in place. The first new tab after turning the option on used to show "No painting could be loaded yet" for good; it now shows the first painting that is ready as soon as it is. Discreet buttons. "Another painting", "Open the record" and "Plain start page" are small, frameless text links, faint until the pointer is on them.

Wren 0.7.0 Wren 0.7.0 runs on Linux as it does on Windows: it builds, installs, updates itself and starts on NixOS. Pages also load and run faster, and the JavaScript heap is smaller. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Linux: wrentool build makes every variant on Linux. H.264 videos play, the windows carry the app id wren, the page fonts follow fontconfig, and a second start of a profile no longer takes the running Wren for a crash. NixOS: Setup makes the installed copy start by itself, without steam-run. Faster pages: script functions that never run cost almost nothing to load, garbage collection stops a page for far less time, and the style work is smaller when the DOM changes. A smaller JavaScript heap: an object takes 40 bytes, and the collector reads only what dies. Text: CSS Text Decoration 3 and 4 in full, highlight pseudo-elements as CSS Pseudo 4 paints them, and text fragments (#:~:text=). The browser: Ctrl+Shift+T reopens the previous session after a restart, a link's address shows over the page, and the frame rate is a choice in the View menu. The documentation site: a menu, a search and a breadcrumb, and tables that scroll sideways on a phone.

Wren 0.7.1 Wren 0.7.1 fixes what the first days of Wren on Linux showed: sound plays through PipeWire, Invidious videos play, and wren ctl works from any shell. This is still a beta, under development. Highlights Sound on Linux: the audio output opens through PipeWire's ALSA plugin, where every video and sound played silent. Videos: an Invidious video plays (XMLHttpRequest reads the body as it arrives), a video keeps its shape in its box, and the bands around it show the element's background. A settings page (about:settings), the toolkit's themes with the system's light or dark, and a machined style. A centred address bar (browser.address_bar.sizing_mode), and a right click on the free space of the title bar opens the toolbar's menu. Bookmarks move sooner when you drag them along the bar.

Remote control: wren ctl Drive a running Wren from a script: navigate, wait, run script, send mouse and keyboard input, read the console and the network log, and capture the window without the screen. The client is a sub-command of wren.exe itself (one file, so client and server always speak the same protocol version). build\wren.exe ctl run --size 1280x800 --shot out.png https://example.com/ # one call: start, load, capture, close About 0.5 s for the whole call on a development build (process start 55 ms, first frame and load 215 ms, capture 70 ms, close 110 ms), against 2 to 3 s for starting Wren, waiting a fixed time and capturing the screen. b: Shaders in the browser's own pages (-wren-shader) The license card of about:wren is lit by a real fragment shader reading a real normal map, not by layers of CSS. The toolkit gives Wren an application shader API (gui_toolkit 0.25.0, its docs/shaders.md: render.create_app_shader, draw.app_shader, render.create_texture_data); this page is what Wren builds on it. The property .base { -wren-shader: card-foil var(--sweep) var(--bx) var(--by) var(--live) 1; } -wren-shader: none | <name> <argument>*. An argument is a <number>, a <percentage> (its value divided by 100) or a calc() of numbers, at most 28. Not inherited, paint only (a change of the arguments never asks for a layout). The shader fills the box's background painting area (the clip of its bottom background layer, rounded by border-radius) over its CSS background and before its border and its content: what the CSS draws is also what shows when the shader cannot be had. The arguments are written with var() on purpose. SharedArrayBuffer and WebAssembly threads A page and its workers can share memory: postMessage of a SharedArrayBuffer or of a shared WebAssembly.Memory gives the same bytes, Atomics.wait and Atomics.notify work between them and with memory.atomic.wait and notify of a module, and a WebAssembly.Module goes to a worker without being compiled again. An Emscripten build with pthreads needs all of that. Where the bytes are Each realm is an instance of the JavaScript engine image, whose objects live in its own linear memory; no pointer in it can reach another's. So a shared buffer's bytes are outside every realm: a Wasmtime shared memory (src/wasm/user_shared.odin). A module reaches them by its instructions, at full speed. A script reaches them through a host buffer (Buffer_Host in src/engine/jsrt): data == nil, one element is one call to the browser, and the JIT and the fast paths step aside. new SharedArrayBuffer makes such a memory too (Host_Shared, config.host_shared), a whole number of pages holding a length in bytes. test262's image keeps the engine's own SharedArrayBuffers: its agents are not realms. So the JavaScript engine's image did not have to be built with threads, and a realm that crashes still loses only itself. Updates Wren can install a new release itself. It never does so without you pressing "Install the update" in About Wren (or running the command of that name), and it only installs a program that Froment Software signed. How it works Check. "Check for updates" (or the daily check, off by default: browser.update.check_daily) asks GitHub for the latest release. Verify. For a newer release, Wren fetches update-windows-x64.json and update-windows-x64.json.sig. It checks, in this order: the Ed25519 signature with the update key built into Wren; that the manifest is for this platform; that its version is the one announced; that it is strictly newer than this program (no downgrade). Install. The program is downloaded to memory; its length, then its SHA-256, must be the signed ones. It is written beside the program (wren.exe.update), read back and compared again; then the running file is renamed to wren.exe.old and the new one renamed in. If any step fails, the old program stays as it was. Restart. The new version runs at the next start; the .old file is deleted then. Limits Windows only for now. On Linux Wren checks and tells you where the file is. Development and labelled builds are not releases: they are updated by hand. The update key is not the license key. Publishing Wren on winget Wren can be offered through the Windows Package Manager (winget), so that winget install FromentSoftware.Wren installs it. This is not automatic: a published release does not reach winget on its own. The step below makes the manifest; the submission to Microsoft's winget-pkgs repository is a manual pull request, and only Sacha does it. There is no Microsoft Store package (the Store needs an MSIX and a developer account; the release is a single portable .exe, which winget supports directly as a portable installer). What the release is Every release publishes one file, wren-<version>-windows-x64.exe (see wrentool package and .github\workflows\release.yml), plus SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256. It is not an installer: it is the program itself, which carries its licenses, its version and the Visual C++ runtime it needs, and integrates into the desktop from within (Setup). So the winget installer type is portable: winget downloads the .exe, keeps it, and adds a link named wren to its own links folder (on the PATH), so wren launches it from a terminal. 1.
